analysis.one_liner: Banned selling national forest timber for less than it costs taxpayers, and helped timber towns adjust.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a Senate Agriculture subcommittee without ever reaching a vote; it had one sponsor and zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal government has long sold timber from national forests for less than the cost of preparing and administering the sales, meaning taxpayers cover the difference. This bill would phase out those below-cost sales, ending a multi-year subsidy to timber buyers, and would spend federal money to help towns and workers who depend on that timber find other work and businesses. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund the gap between what national forest timber sells for and what it costs the government to make it available. Timber workers and their communities also benefit from the bill's grants, loans, and retraining programs designed to ease the transition away from subsidized logging.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Forest Service from making below-cost timber sales, phasing in the ban over five years and fully applying it starting October 1, 1997 [S3].
Requires the Forest Service to identify national forest lands that lose money on timber and remove them from the timber base for at least 10 years [S3].
Authorizes grants, low-interest loans, and training for community development corporations, displaced timber workers' families, and cooperatives in timber-dependent communities [S3].
Requires reforestation deposits to come from net forest revenues rather than from other appropriated funds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber buyers — mills and logging companies that purchased below-cost national forest timber — would pay market-cost prices or lose access to money-losing sales. Taxpayers also fund the bill's transition assistance programs.

drawbacks.text: The phase-in allows below-cost sales to continue for years: through fiscal 1997, and at shrinking volumes (75%, then 65%, then 50% of prior-year sales) before the full ban takes effect [S3].
Title II authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in appropriations for transition assistance with no dollar cap [S3].
Communities where mills depend on national forest timber for half or more of their supply could see mill closures if money-losing sales end, even with transition aid [S3].
Violating regulations under Title I carries criminal penalties of 6 months to 1 year imprisonment, an unusually heavy enforcement tool for forest management rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ending below-cost timber sales is a straightforward taxpayer win — the government stops selling a public resource at a loss. The cost is real but targeted: timber communities lose subsidized sales, and the bill's own answer is a decade of transition spending for the affected towns. The main design weakness is the slow phase-in, which lets the subsidy drain continue well past enactment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, referred to a subcommittee that never acted, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyche Fowler introduced the bill on June 19, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S1].
On September 10, 1991, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry, where no further action was taken [S5].
The bill received no floor vote, no hearing record in the sources, and expired at the end of the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry kept its access to below-cost national forest timber, and taxpayers kept covering the losses on those sales for the remainder of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber buyers kept their subsidized timber

for.name: Sen. Wyche Fowler, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Forest Timber Sales Cost Recovery Act of 1991 to eliminate below-cost timber sales and fund transition aid for timber-dependent communities.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over national forest management
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry on September 10, 1991, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Timber and wood-products industry
against.role: Industry that purchased below-cost national forest timber
against.what_they_did: Defended the continued availability of below-cost timber sales from national forests during this period, opposing cost-recovery proposals.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.note: Below-cost sales let mills buy national forest timber for less than the government spends producing it — a subsidy paid by taxpayers. The bill ends that subsidy over five years and removes money-losing lands from the timber base.
Communities where mills draw half their timber from national forest sales could lose supply and jobs, but the bill funds community development grants, loans, and worker retraining to ease the shift.
